llm_note: The edition title and translation credit support an identifiable selected-works volume. The description combines part of Candide, three stories, philosophical selections, other writings, and thirty-five letters, establishing a mixed author collection rather than a bounded fiction collection. The 1948 edition date and frozen first-publish year do not establish the original dates of the underlying contents.

The 1929 subtitle identifies a bounded collection of five named fictional works, selected and edited by H. C. Harwood. The 2010 title and subtitle, 'The amazing journeys of Jules Verne: five visionary classics,' are compatible with that collection, although their contents are not supplied to confirm equivalence. The 1929 edition explicitly reprints existing books; neither its date nor the frozen first-publish year establishes the original dates of those contents.

The 1901 subtitle, 'seven of her lays done into English,' identifies a real multi-text collection rather than an author-heading artifact. The 2015 subtitle 'Poetry' is compatible, although it does not confirm identical contents. Poetry metadata supports classification as another literary form despite the Legends and Romances subjects. The 1901 date concerns a translated edition and does not establish when the underlying lays originated.

The shared author-name title groups distinct collections: 'letters from England 1813–1844,' 'chosen letters,' and 'selections from her works.' These are not clearly manifestations of one stable collection. Letter collections dominate, but the unspecified selections and generic Fiction subject leave the cluster's content type unclear. The explicit 1813–1844 correspondence dates support underlying contents outside the target window; the frozen 1910 date identifies an edition of selections, not demonstrated original composition or publication.

The 1944 edition identifies a bounded collection of twenty-four representative stories selected and introduced by Henry Seidel Canby. The Fiction subject supports a fiction collection, and the identically titled 1980 edition is compatible with a later manifestation. The frozen first-publish year of 1944, corroborated by the detailed 1944 edition, supports an in-window date for the collection.

All three editions bear the same title, Complete stories, supporting one coherent story collection; the Fiction subject supports primarily fictional contents. The frozen first-publish year of 1941 agrees with the earliest supplied edition, supporting an in-window origin for the collection, though individual stories' original dates are not supplied.

The 1947 and 1950 editions plausibly represent one collection of twenty stories and seven poems, but the cluster also includes 'Selected Stories' and 'illustrated poems,' indicating materially different author collections. Poetry and short-story subjects support an author-centered, mixed-form grouping rather than one stable fiction collection. The 1947 first-publish metadata dates a collected edition, not reliably the original contents; the supplied evidence does not establish their original publication dates.

The editions appear to combine different author collections: 'poetry & prose' (1939, 1946), 'Poems' in Everyman's editions, and 'poetical works' (1966). These indicate differing content scope rather than clearly interchangeable manifestations of one collection. The subtitles support poetry and mixed author selections, not fiction, despite the general fiction subject. The 1939 first-publish metadata dates a collection edition but does not establish when its underlying contents originated.

The description and two editions identify a five-novel omnibus, while two other editions explicitly identify Selected Short Stories, indicating materially different collections rather than manifestations of one collection. The identified contents are fiction. The unsubtitled 1934 edition does not establish the omnibus's identity or its contents' original dates; the 1934 first-publish field and later edition dates therefore do not reliably establish the original date window.

The description identifies a three-novel fiction collection matching the 1998 editions titled Three Gothic novels. The remaining editions are titled only Novels, without contents establishing whether they represent the same selection or a substantially different collection. Collection identity therefore remains uncertain. The description explicitly dates the named novels to 1798–1799; the 1887 first-publish field and later edition dates do not establish an original work within the target window.

The record combines multi-volume collected editions with separate portions of The Jewish War and Jewish Antiquities, plus differently scoped selections such as The Essential Works and The Essential Writings. These do not establish one stable collection. The contents are broad historical and apologetic writings, despite incidental fiction subjects. The description dates an underlying work to about AD 78 and Antiquities roughly sixteen years later; 1926 is a modern edition date, not the original content date.

The editions combine materially different collections and works: A Choice of Kipling's Verse, Complete Verse, Departmental Ditties, The Seven Seas, Stories from India, and Something of Myself and Other Autobiographical Writings. These are not manifestations of one stable collection. Although the description emphasizes poetry, the cluster also includes fiction, autobiography, and selected works. Poems, 1886–1929 explicitly supports an in-window origin for the principal verse contents; the frozen 1899 date does not establish a common original date for the entire cluster.

The editions combine Azul, Cantos de vida y esperanza, Eleven poems, complete poetry, selected poetry, and semblanza y florilegio volumes, alongside compilations combining separately titled works. These are materially different works and collections, not manifestations of one stable Poems collection. The aggregate spans poetry, prose stories, and broader author selections. The 1888 Azul edition supports an in-window date for that component, but neither it nor the frozen first-publish year establishes an original date for the heterogeneous entity as a whole.

The edition title, 'Bernie Babcock: an appreciation,' supports a bounded publication about the author rather than an author-heading artifact or fiction collection. The subtitle and 'Catalogs' subject outweigh the generic 'Fiction' subject for content classification. The 1923 edition and matching frozen first-publish year support an in-window origin, though the original publication date is not independently confirmed.

Edition subtitles identify materially different works and selections: The Legend of Good Women, individual Canterbury Tales, a Canterbury Tales/Troilus and Criseyde selection, CD-ROM manuals, and Sources and Backgrounds. These do not represent one stable work or collection, and their content types vary. The subject identifying Chaucer as deceased by 1400 supports an origin outside the date window for the underlying literary texts; the frozen 1888 date reflects a later publication rather than their original composition.

The description identifies a 32-poem illustrated selection, but editions include materially different poetry collections, hitherto unpublished prose, Four Complete Novels, The Complete Shorter Fiction, biographical material, and Treasure Island study notes. These are not manifestations of one stable collection, and their content types differ substantially. The frozen 1896 date and listed edition dates do not establish a common original intellectual-work date for this heterogeneous cluster.

The editions consistently identify Diana: A Strange Autobiography, with only subtitle omission or series information varying, supporting one coherent work. Explicit Fiction, lesbian fiction, and LGBTQ fiction before Stonewall subjects favor a fictional narrative, although the autobiography subtitle and Biography subject leave genre ambiguity. The matching 1939 first-publish metadata and several 1939 editions support an original date within the target window.

The shared author-name title groups materially different publications: complete works, selected works, a presentation and anthology, critical studies ('une étude'), illustrated poems, and 'A Season in Hell.' These do not plausibly represent one stable work or collection. Subjects emphasize poetry and criticism, but the cluster has no stable content scope. The 1921 first-publish date corresponds to 'Leben und Dichtung' and does not establish an original date for the other works or collected contents.

The edition subtitle, 'selected short stories,' identifies a bounded fiction collection rather than an author-heading artifact or broad mixed-genre oeuvre. The Fiction and Translations into English subjects reinforce this reading. The 1922 edition date and frozen first-publish year date the selection's publication but do not establish when its underlying stories originated.

The Work title and sole edition title, Works, plausibly identify a collected edition of Wilkie Collins published by P. F. Collier in 1899, rather than a heading artifact. The broad title supports an author-works collection; the Fiction subject suggests fictional contents but does not establish a bounded fiction collection. No contents or description are supplied, and the 1899 edition date does not reliably establish the original dates of the underlying works.

Both editions identify the same publication, Maria Edgeworth: selections from her works, with the same publisher and 1910 date. This supports a coherent author-selection volume rather than a person-heading artifact or specific fiction work. The Fiction subject does not establish a bounded fiction collection. The 1910 edition dates and frozen first-publish year do not establish when the selected contents originally appeared.

The editions consistently identify Steinbeck/The Portable Steinbeck, including the 1943 volume selected by Pascal Covici, supporting a coherent author anthology rather than a heading artifact. The description combines stories, novel excerpts, a complete novel, nonfiction selections, and a Nobel acceptance speech, establishing broad mixed-genre scope. The frozen 1943 first-publication year, matching selected-volume editions, and current 1946 date support an anthology origin within 1880–1950, though the described contents may reflect later expansion.

Edition subtitles identify materially different publications: 'Stories and Fairy Tales,' 'Oeuvres, tome 2,' 'His Poems and the Story of His Life,' and 'The Complete Fairy Tales and Stories.' Subjects also span fiction, biography, correspondence, and musicals. These support a heterogeneous cluster rather than one stable collection. The 1942 first-publish field matches the edition subtitled 'the maker of fairy tales ...' but does not establish the original dates of the other underlying works or contents.

The matching edition titles plausibly identify one collection, with the subtitle 'Best Short Stories' and subject 'Fiction, general' supporting primarily fictional contents rather than an author-heading artifact. The unsubtitled edition leaves some uncertainty about collection scope. The 1943 first-publish metadata and 1943/1946 edition dates do not reliably establish the original date of the collection or its contents.

The shared title masks materially different publications: autobiography, letters to Benson and Monod, A Life in Letters, critical essays, essays on art and drama, Collected Stories, Selected Tales, and The Spoils of Poynton. These are not manifestations of one stable collection. The description concerns an annotated correspondence selection and does not cover the full cluster, which mixes fiction, autobiography, correspondence, and criticism. The frozen 1930 date and current 1964 date correspond to different publications and do not establish a single original intellectual-work date.

All four editions share the title Long Lance and plausibly represent one work. The 1928 edition explicitly identifies it as 'the autobiography of a Blackfoot Indian chief,' supporting autobiographical form despite conflicting fiction subjects. The frozen and current first-publication metadata both give 1928, corroborated by two 1928 editions and a 1929 edition.

Most editions represent Her Life, Letters, and Journals, edited by Ednah D. Cheney, but the cluster also includes Little Women; Little Men; Jo's Boys, Selected Fiction, Works of Louisa May Alcott, and An Intimate Anthology. These are materially different works or collections, mixing biography and personal writings with fiction. The childhood-diary description does not describe the whole cluster. Multiple 1889 editions support an early date for the life-and-letters volume, but neither that date nor the current 1995 first-publish field establishes a common original date for the heterogeneous contents.

The shared title 'Charles Lamb' and the 2012 edition's subtitle 'Selected Writings' plausibly identify an author-selected-writings collection, rather than a person-heading artifact or specific fiction work. No edition title clearly indicates a different work, although identical contents are not established. The generic fiction subject does not establish a fiction-only collection. The frozen 1949 first-publish year and dated Viking edition do not establish when the underlying writings originated.

The Work and sole edition share the title Fairy tales, and the children's stories and juvenile fiction subjects support a coherent fiction collection. No conflicting titles are supplied, though the collection's contents are unspecified. The 1894 Lippincott edition and frozen first-publish year do not establish when the underlying tales originally appeared.

The sole edition is titled Sassoon, published by Penguin Publishing Group in 1949, with no subtitle or description identifying its contents. The broad subject 'Fiction, general' does not establish whether this is a specific fictional work, a collection, or an author anthology. The eponymous title alone does not justify treating it as a heading artifact. The edition date and frozen first-publish year do not reliably establish the original date of the underlying contents.

The edition title matches the Work title, and its subtitle, 'a thrilling romance,' together with the subject 'English fiction,' supports a specific fictional narrative rather than an author-heading artifact. The 1889 edition date and frozen first-publish year agree, but neither independently establishes the original intellectual-work date.

All three editions share the title [Works] and publisher Scribner, with compatible dates of 1934 and [1929–1934], supporting a coherent collected edition rather than an author-heading artifact. The generic title suggests collected author works; the Fiction and Forsyte-family subjects do not establish a specifically bounded fiction collection. The frozen 1929 first-publish year and edition dates do not reliably date the original constituent works.

The description identifies The Portable Poe, and the edition titles plausibly represent variants and reprints of the same collection selected by Philip Van Doren Stern. Its contents include tales, poetry, letters, articles, criticism, and opinions, making it a broad mixed-author anthology rather than a fiction-only collection. The 1945 first-publish metadata and editions date the collected volume but do not establish the original dates of its underlying writings.

The edition subtitle identifies a coherent mixed-author collection containing memoirs, Tristram Shandy, A Sentimental Journey, and selected sermons and letters. The eponymous title is therefore not merely a heading artifact. The description covers only Tristram Shandy and does not establish the scope of the whole volume. The 1950 publication date and frozen first-publish year date this edition, not reliably the original constituent works.

The subtitles identify Leucippe and Clitophon / The Adventures of Leucippe and Clitophon, supporting one specific romance behind the author-name title. Greek romance and love-story subjects, English-translation labeling, and compatible edition titles support a coherent fiction work rather than an author heading or collection. The classical-library context suggests an older Greek original; 1917 appears to date the translated edition, not the underlying narrative.

Six editions plausibly represent the mixed-author-form collection Charles Lamb: prose & poetry, including a version with essays by Hazlitt and De Quincey. The 1965 Dawson's Book Shop title Charles Lamb: bibliophile appears to identify a materially different publication, making the overall cluster heterogeneous rather than a heading artifact. The 1921 first-publish year and edition dates do not establish when the underlying collected writings originated.

The sole edition, titled Lamb and published in 1924, matches the Work title but does not establish its contents or bibliographic form. The description of Martha the talking dog and the subjects Dogs, Juvenile fiction, and Soups conflict with the frozen Charles Lamb attribution, suggesting mismatched metadata. Neither a stable collection nor a specific fictional work can be identified confidently; the 1924 edition date does not establish the original intellectual-work date.

The editions combine distinct poetry collections, including Poems, 1938–1945, Collected poems, 1914–1947, Poems, 1968–1970, and Poems, 1970–1972, alongside selected and complete poems. Two editions also identify the separate fiction pairing of The Story of Marie/Mary Powell and The Islands of Unwisdom. Poetry is the primary literary form, but this is not one stable collection. Explicit content ranges span both sides of 1950, so the frozen 1925 date cannot establish a single original-work date for the cluster.

The consistently titled editions and recurring publishers plausibly represent one stable collected volume, not an author-heading artifact. Edition 10 explicitly combines translated Petronius with Seneca's Apocolocyntosis, supporting a multi-work classical-author collection rather than one specific fiction work. The Latin-satire and ancient Roman subjects support ancient underlying contents; the frozen 1913 date and later publication dates concern translated editions, not original composition.

The editions divide between Four complete novels and Five complete novels, including a series II designation, suggesting distinct omnibus collections rather than manifestations of one stable collection. The titles and Western stories subject support fiction collections. The frozen 1940 first-publish year and one June 1940 edition date do not reliably establish the original dates of the constituent novels; the other editions date from 1980–1987.

The shared author-name title groups materially different selections: passages with a life sketch and reading guide, representative selections, selected essays, essays and journals, and selected essays, lectures and poems. These support a cluster of distinct Emerson anthologies rather than one stable collection. The description and multi-form collected-works subject establish broad author selections. The 1902 frozen date and later edition dates do not reliably date either the underlying writings or a single identifiable compilation.

The two editions have compatible eponymous titles, the same publisher, and 1918 publication dates. Edition 2's subtitle explicitly explains that the author's name serves as the book title and identifies him as a writer of stories, supporting a real fiction collection rather than an author-heading artifact. Fiction subjects reinforce this reading. The frozen first-publish year and both edition dates support an original collection date of 1918.

All five edition titles consistently identify Collected stories; the Penguin Modern Classics wording is compatible with a later edition of the same collection. Subjects explicitly identify short stories and fiction by one author. The frozen first-publish year of 1945 is corroborated by two Constable editions dated 1945, supporting an in-window origin for the collection, though individual stories' original dates are not supplied.

The shared title 'Cervantes' masks materially different compilations: 'the Selected Works,' 'selections from his works,' 'An Alphabet of Quijote,' and 'prologues and epilogue.' These do not plausibly identify one stable collection. The evidence indicates broad author selections and mixed forms rather than one fiction work or bounded fiction collection. The frozen 1923 date and edition dates establish publication of these compilations, not the original dates of their underlying contents.

The description identifies a thematic selection of Lamb's essays, dramatic criticism, verse, and letters, consistent with the edition subtitle 'Selected Writings.' The eponymous edition titles are compatible with a real collection, although equivalence between the 1949 Viking and 2003 Routledge selections is not established. Lamb's supplied lifespan (1775–1834) and the description's reference to his 1807 writing place the underlying contents before 1880; the 1949 date concerns the collection's publication, not the original writings.

Edition subtitles identify materially different publications: selected poems, novel omnibuses, short-story collections, selected literary criticism, a composite biography, reminiscences and correspondence, critical essays, and a rare-book catalogue. These cannot plausibly be manifestations of one stable collection. The poetry description covers only part of the cluster. The frozen 1928 date corresponds to selected-poem editions and does not establish an original date for the heterogeneous record.

The shared title 'Gray' and compatible subtitles 'Poems and Letters' and 'Poetry and Prose' plausibly identify a coherent author collection spanning literary forms, rather than a specific fiction work. These explicit subtitles outweigh the generic fiction subject. The 1926 and 1955 edition dates and frozen first-publish year do not establish when the underlying contents originated.

Edition subtitles identify distinct works: On Diseases and Symptoms, On Antecedent Causes, and On the Properties of Foodstuffs. The description concerns only the last, a translation and commentary on Galen's physiological treatise De alimentorum facultatibus. These are different medical/philosophical works, not manifestations of one work or a stable collection; the isolated Fiction subject does not outweigh this evidence. The ancient intellectual contents fall outside 1880–1950; the 1937 frozen date and modern edition dates do not establish their original publication dates.
